hook: Snowball or thermostat? Sort 6 everyday loops.
title: Snowball or Thermostat?

game.prompt: Does this settle back like a thermostat (←) or keep growing like a snowball (→)?

items.text: Short on sleep, you scroll late to unwind, then sleep even less
items.why: Tired leads to scrolling leads to more tired. Vicious circles are reinforcing too.

items.text: Money in savings earns interest, which earns more interest
items.why: Growth feeds more growth. Classic reinforcing loop.

items.text: You feel hungry, eat, and the hunger goes away
items.why: Your body pulls you back toward a set point. That's balancing.

items.text: A rumor spreads: the more people know, the more people tell
items.why: Each new teller makes more tellers, whether the rumor is true or false.

items.text: You speed up when late, slow down once you're on time
items.why: The gap to a goal drives the action, and the action closes the gap.

items.text: Practicing makes it easier, so you practice more
items.why: Virtuous circle: skill makes practice pleasant, practice builds skill.

insight: Snowball loops amplify, good or bad. Thermostat loops pull back to a target. It's a thinking tool from systems science, not a lab finding. Know which loop you're in before you push.
model: Reinforcing loops snowball; balancing loops hold a set point. Ask which one is running.
try_today: Write one habit you want as a loop: 'A makes B, B makes more A.' Find the arrow you can strengthen today.
try_team: With your team, class or family: each person names one loop in your shared life. Vote: snowball or thermostat? Pick one to feed or break this week.

hook: One skipped walk can turn into a lost month. Where would you cut it?
title: Cut the Vicious Circle

steps.scenario: The loop: low energy, so you skip your walk. Moving less, you sleep a bit worse. Worse sleep, even less energy. Which link is easiest to cut today?

options.text: Fix my energy first, then start walking again
options.feedback: Waiting to feel ready is how the loop keeps running. Energy often follows movement, not the other way round.

options.text: A 5-minute walk, even feeling flat
options.feedback: Yes. Tiny and doable on a bad day. One small action can turn the same circle the other way.

options.text: Plan a full new fitness routine for Monday
options.feedback: Big plans feel good, but they start later and ask for energy you don't have yet.

steps.scenario: A week later the loop is turning the good way, then you miss two days. You think…

options.text: "Ruined. Back to square one."
options.feedback: Understandable, but loops don't reset to zero. Calling it ruined is what restarts the downward lap.

options.text: "Two days off. Short walk today and the loop keeps turning."
options.feedback: Right. A loop is about direction, not a perfect streak. Nudge it back the good way.

insight: Spirals can feel like bad luck or a flaw in you, but often they're just a loop. Draw the circle and you see each link. You don't fix it all, just one arrow.
model: If it keeps getting worse (or better) on its own, look for the circle, then cut or feed one link.
try_today: Sketch one loop in your life as 4 boxes and arrows. Circle the easiest link and change just that one today.
try_team: Draw a loop your group keeps falling into (late starts, messy kitchen, missed homework). Everyone marks the easiest link. Change that one for a week.

hook: Why do you always end up scalding, then freezing, in a new shower?
title: The Shower Problem

steps.scenario: Hotel shower. Water is cold. You turn the knob toward hot. Five seconds later it's still cold. You…

options.text: Crank it much hotter. It clearly isn't working.
options.feedback: Very human, and exactly how you get scalded. The hot water was already in the pipe, on its way.

options.text: Wait a few more seconds before touching it again
options.feedback: Yes. The pipe adds a delay. Give your last action time to show its result.

options.text: Give up and take a cold shower
options.feedback: Brave, but the system was working. It was just slow to report back.

steps.scenario: Three weeks into a new workout plan, you don't feel much different yet. You…

options.text: Double the intensity to force results
options.feedback: That's the shower move again. Overcorrecting raises the risk of injury or burnout.

options.text: Keep the plan and judge it again after 8 weeks
options.feedback: Bodies, skills, and relationships all respond with a lag. Set a fair review date.

options.text: Switch to a totally different plan
options.feedback: Switching resets the clock before the first plan could show anything.

insight: When results lag behind actions, it feels like nothing works, so we push harder. Then the late results land and we overshoot. Many problems are delay problems, not effort problems.
model: Slow feedback plus impatience equals overshoot. Act, wait for the lag, then adjust.
try_today: Pick one thing you're trying to improve. Write how long it fairly takes to show results, and set a reminder for that date.

source.work: The Fifth Discipline (1990); Sterman, Business Dynamics (2000)

try_team: Before changing a plan, ask the group: how long should this take to show results? Agree a review date and don't touch the knob before it.

from_source.cite: Peter Senge, The Fifth Discipline (1990), ch. 4 'The Laws of the Fifth Discipline'
from_source.next_read: The Fifth Discipline, ch. 4, then ch. 5 'A Shift of Mind' on balancing loops and delays

hook: Smart people, one small change, total chaos. Who's to blame?
title: The Beer Game

game.prompt: Shop → wholesaler → distributor → factory. Deliveries take weeks. Shoppers go from 4 cases a week to 8, then stay at 8. What do the orders do?
choices: Orders rise smoothly to 8 and stay there
Orders swing between huge and almost none
game.reveal: They swing wildly. Stock is slow to arrive, so players keep ordering, then drown in it and stop. If you picked 'smoothly', that's what nearly everyone expects. Afterwards, many players blamed wild customer demand. It had changed once. Your version: texting "??" three times before the first reply has even landed, then getting four replies at once.

insight: In MIT's Beer Game, played since the 1960s, smart people make the same swings again and again. The cause isn't who plays. It's the delay built into the chain.
model: When everyone overreacts, look for the delay before you look for someone to blame.
try_today: Sent a message or made a request? Wait for it to land before you send it again.
try_team: When a problem in your group swings back and forth, draw the chain on paper and mark every delay. Agree to change one thing at a time.

source.work: Sterman, 'Modeling Managerial Behavior: Misperceptions of Feedback in a Dynamic Decision Making Experiment', Management Science (1989); Senge, The Fifth Discipline (1990)

from_source.cite: Peter Senge, The Fifth Discipline (1990), ch. 3 'Prisoners of the System, or Prisoners of Our Own Thinking?'
from_source.next_read: The Fifth Discipline, ch. 3 (the full Beer Game story and its three lessons)

hook: Most people push where change is hardest. Can you find the lever?
title: Where to Push

game.prompt: You want to stop doomscrolling at night. Rank these fixes from weakest to strongest lever.
items: Information: a screen-time report of your real hours
Rules: phone charges outside your bedroom
Goals: judge nights by how rested you feel
Mindset: scrolling stops feeling like rest
game.explain: 1 Numbers: easy to change, rarely sticks. 2 Information: you see the real cost. 3 Rules: the setup does the work. 4 Goals: redefine a good night. 5 Mindset: changes what you want. Meadows ranked 12 such levers.

insight: Adjusting numbers rarely changes how a system behaves. Changing who sees what, the rules, or the goal moves more with less force. Meadows called her list a draft, not a law.
model: Numbers are easy and weak. Information, rules, and goals are harder and strong.
try_today: Pick one stuck problem. Instead of 'more' or 'less' of something, write one change to its rules, information, or goal.

source.work: Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System (1999)

try_team: At your next meeting, class council or family talk, ask 'what are we actually rewarded for?' before asking anyone to try harder.

from_source.quote: Give me a place to stand, and I will move the earth.
from_source.cite: Archimedes, as reported by Pappus of Alexandria, Collection, Book 8 (traditional English rendering)
from_source.next_read: Donella Meadows, Thinking in Systems (2008), ch. 6 'Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System', especially her warning that leverage points are counterintuitive

hook: When stuck, do you try harder or change the game? Find out.
title: Tweaker or Redesigner?

questions.q: You keep spending too much. Your first move is…

options.label: Promise to be stricter with myself
Track every purchase for a month
Make savings move automatically on payday

questions.q: Your group project keeps missing deadlines. You…

options.label: Make progress visible to everyone each week
Ask what each person is really rewarded for

questions.q: You want to read more. You…

options.label: Put a book where your phone usually sits
Just try to remember to read

questions.q: The same argument with a friend, sibling or partner keeps coming back. You…

options.label: Prepare my points better for next time
Agree a pause rule when it starts
Ask what each of you is actually trying to protect

zones.label: Tweaker
zones.text: Today's answers reach for effort and numbers first. Honest work, but tiring. Next time, ask: what rule, information, or goal is producing this?

zones.label: Switch-hitter
zones.text: Today's answers switch between pushing harder and redesigning. Notice which one you grab under stress, and try the redesign first once this week.

zones.label: Redesigner
zones.text: Today's answers look for the structure behind the problem. Keep going, and give redesigns time: their results also arrive late.

insight: Meadows ranked 'numbers' (targets, budgets) among the weakest levers; we add willpower to that list. Changing what people see, what's rewarded, or the goal tends to work with less strain.
model: Before pushing harder, ask what structure is producing the result.
try_today: Take one 'I should try harder' and rewrite it as a change to your surroundings, rules, or reminders. Do that change now.
try_team: Next time your team or class is stuck, ban 'try harder' for 5 minutes. List changes to what people see, what's rewarded, or the goal.

from_source.quote: Small changes can produce big results
from_source.cite: Peter Senge, The Fifth Discipline (1990), ch. 4 'The Laws of the Fifth Discipline'
from_source.next_read: The Fifth Discipline, ch. 4; then Meadows, Thinking in Systems (2008), ch. 6

hook: A city paid people per rat tail. Guess what it got more of.
title: The Rat Tail Bounty

game.prompt: Hanoi, 1902. Rats are spreading through the new sewers, so officials pay a small bounty for every rat tail handed in. What happens next?
game.reveal: It backfired. People were seen with live rats missing only their tails, so the rats kept breeding, and there were reports of rats being farmed for tails. Historian Michael Vann documented it. If you guessed 'rats disappear', that's what the officials expected too: the fix rewarded tails, not fewer rats.

insight: A quick fix eases the symptom today, while its side effect quietly feeds the problem. The side effect is late, so the fix looks like it works, and we repeat it.
model: Ask of every fix: what does this reward, and what will it feed in three months?
try_today: Name one quick fix you use often (snacking, cramming, avoiding). Write what it might be feeding in the long run.

source.work: The Fifth Discipline (1990); Vann, 'Of Rats, Rice, and Race' (2003)

try_team: Pick one rule or reward your group uses (points, chores, targets). Spend 5 minutes asking: how could someone game this, and what would that feed?

from_source.cite: Peter Senge, The Fifth Discipline (1990), ch. 4 'The Laws of the Fifth Discipline'
from_source.next_read: The Fifth Discipline, ch. 4; Meadows, Thinking in Systems (2008), ch. 5 'System Traps... and Opportunities'

hook: The fix worked on Monday. Why is the problem bigger by Friday?
title: Spot the Backfire

steps.scenario: You sleep until noon on Sunday to catch up after a late Saturday. What's the hidden side effect?

options.text: None, you've paid back the sleep
options.feedback: You do get rest. But your body clock also shifts later, and that bill arrives on Sunday night.

options.text: Sunday night you can't fall asleep, so Monday hurts
options.feedback: Right. The lie-in eases today's tiredness and pushes your clock later. Researchers call the mismatch 'social jet lag'.

steps.scenario: Homework's due in an hour (or a work task you don't really get), so you copy a mate's answers. What grows?

options.text: Nothing, it's handed in
options.feedback: Real relief tonight. But the gap in what you understand keeps growing underneath.

options.text: The bit you don't understand, which shows up in the test
options.feedback: Yes. The fix ends tonight's panic and feeds next month's.

steps.scenario: Plot twist from real life: Mexico City, 1989. To cut smog, each car is banned from driving one weekday, based on its number plate. What did many families do?

options.text: Took the bus on their banned day
options.feedback: That was the plan. But a cheaper way round it was sitting in the used-car market.

options.text: Bought a second car, often an older one
options.feedback: Yes. Car numbers rose, many extra cars were old and dirtier, and economist Lucas Davis found no clear drop in air pollution.

options.text: Drove less on every day of the week
options.feedback: A hopeful guess. The rule only touched one day, so it changed which car, not how much driving.

insight: Every fix has a main effect and a side effect. The main effect shows up fast; the side effect arrives later and often feeds the problem you were fixing.
model: Before a quick fix, ask: what will this feed when no one is watching?
try_today: Take one fix you used this week (lie-in, snack, cramming). Write its side effect and one tweak that keeps the relief.
try_team: Before agreeing a new rule at home, school or work, take 5 minutes: each person imagines how a clever lazy person would get round it.

source.work: The Fifth Discipline (1990); Davis, 'The Effect of Driving Restrictions on Air Quality in Mexico City', Journal of Political Economy (2008); Wittmann, Dinich, Merrow & Roenneberg, 'Social Jetlag', Chronobiology International (2006)

from_source.quote: Behavior grows better before it grows worse.
from_source.cite: Peter Senge, The Fifth Discipline (1990), ch. 4 'The Laws of the Fifth Discipline'
from_source.next_read: The Fifth Discipline, ch. 4, then Appendix 2 on the 'Fixes That Fail' archetype

hook: What's your crutch quietly doing to the muscle underneath?
title: Crutch or Muscle?

game.prompt: Does this treat the symptom, or build the real capacity?

items.text: A third coffee every afternoon to get through the slump
items.why: It works today, but it can hurt tonight's sleep, which deepens tomorrow's slump.
If short sleep is behind the slump, this goes after the cause, not the feeling.

items.text: Always getting a parent or friend to make your awkward phone calls
items.why: Relief now, but your own skill and confidence never get the reps.

items.text: Making the awkward call yourself, with them nearby for backup
items.why: Uncomfortable, but each try builds the skill you were avoiding.

items.text: Using autocorrect for a word you never learn to spell
items.why: Harmless here. Not every crutch is bad; just know which muscle you're skipping.

items.text: Asking a teacher to explain the step you keep getting wrong
items.why: Help that teaches is the opposite of a crutch: it shrinks your need for help.

insight: When a quick fix keeps solving a problem for you, your own ability can weaken, so you need the fix more. Help isn't the issue; help that replaces learning is.
model: Use help that teaches. Watch for fixes you need more each month.
try_today: Pick one thing you always outsource or avoid. Do one small piece of it yourself today, with support nearby if you need it.
try_team: Each person names one task they always hand to the same helper. Pair up: the helper coaches, the other does it, once this week.

from_source.quote: The easy way out usually leads back in.
from_source.cite: Peter Senge, The Fifth Discipline (1990), ch. 4 'The Laws of the Fifth Discipline'
from_source.next_read: Meadows, Thinking in Systems (2008), ch. 5, the trap 'Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor'

hook: A group can know more than any member. Does it use what it knows?
title: The Clue Nobody Said

game.prompt: Researchers gave small groups facts about three candidates in a student election. Together each group knew enough to spot the strongest one, but the key facts were split up, a piece per person. What did most groups do?
choices: Pooled the clues and picked the best
Talked about what they all already knew
game.reveal: They mostly talked about what they all already knew. In Stasser and Titus's 1985 study, shared facts got far more airtime than facts only one person held, so few groups picked the best candidate. When everyone got all the facts up front, most did. If you guessed 'pooled the clues', you're in good company: that's what most people expect groups to do.

insight: Groups drift to facts everyone already holds, so the clue only one person has can go unsaid. Being quiet isn't the fix on its own; asking for unshared facts is.
model: Before a group decides, ask: what does only one of us know?
try_today: In your next family, class or work chat about a decision, ask: 'Has anyone noticed something the rest of us haven't?' Then wait.
try_team: Before deciding, each person writes one fact they think only they know. Read them all aloud first, then discuss. Five minutes.

source.work: Stasser & Titus, 'Pooling of Unshared Information in Group Decision Making', Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (1985); Cain, Quiet (2012)

hook: The first voice sets the room. How do you hear the slower ones?
title: Make Room for Slow Thinking

steps.scenario: A teacher asks the class a hard question. Three hands shoot up within a second. What gets more thoughtful answers from more students?

options.text: Call on the first hand to keep things moving
options.feedback: Quick and natural. But then the fastest few do the thinking, and the rest learn they needn't.

options.text: Wait about three silent seconds before calling on anyone
options.feedback: Yes. In Mary Budd Rowe's classroom studies, waiting about 3 seconds led to longer answers and more students joining in.

options.text: Give the answer so nobody feels stuck
options.feedback: Kind, but it skips the thinking. A few seconds of quiet is often all people need.

steps.scenario: Your team or club needs ideas to stop wasting time. The usual way is everyone talking at once. What tends to give more ideas?

options.text: An open brainstorm, loudest ideas first
options.feedback: Lively, but people wait their turn and drop ideas while others talk.

options.text: Everyone writes ideas alone for 5 minutes, then shares
options.feedback: Yes. Diehl and Stroebe (1987) found people working alone, then pooling, had more ideas than groups brainstorming aloud. Waiting your turn blocks ideas.

options.text: Let the most senior person decide quickly
options.feedback: Fast, but you get one view of a problem everyone sees a part of.

steps.scenario: Your group chat (friends, team or family) keeps flaring up into fall-outs. Everyone has a quick theory why. What finds the real pattern?

options.text: Go with whoever's loudest
options.feedback: Loud isn't proof. A pattern that repeats needs the record more than a debate.

options.text: Scroll back and look at when each fall-out actually started
options.feedback: Yes. A pattern hides in any one argument and shows up when you line them up.

options.text: Mute the chat and start a new one
options.feedback: Tempting, but the same pattern usually moves to the new chat with you.

insight: Loud, fast rooms reward the first idea. A short pause, silent writing or a look back at the record lets slower clues surface. That helps everyone think, not just quiet people.
model: Pause before the talk: silence, paper or a look back lets slow patterns show.
try_today: Next time you ask someone a question, count three seconds in your head before you fill the silence.
try_team: Open your next meeting, class or family plan with 3 minutes of silent writing. Go round, one idea each, before open talk.

source.work: Rowe, 'Wait Time: Slowing Down May Be a Way of Speeding Up!', Journal of Teacher Education (1986); Diehl & Stroebe, 'Productivity Loss in Brainstorming Groups: Toward the Solution of a Riddle', JPSP (1987); Cain, Quiet (2012)

hook: You're helping a struggling hire. Could the help be the problem?
title: The Set-Up-to-Fail Loop

game.prompt: A new hire misses one deadline. You start checking their work and ask for daily updates. Six weeks on, what tends to happen?
choices: They play it safe, take less initiative, and slip more
game.reveal: Often the second. Manzoni & Barsoux called it the set-up-to-fail syndrome: close checking signals doubt, the person pulls back, and the boss reads that as proof. If you picked 'improve', that's the hope behind most checking. Both sides feed the loop, usually with good intentions.

insight: Your doubt and their doubt feed each other in a snowball loop. Neither person is the villain; the circle is. Cut one arrow: name the worry and agree a clear way back.
model: Treating someone like they'll fail can help them fail. Look for the loop before you judge the person.
try_today: Pick the person you worry about most. In your next 1:1, ask 'What would help you own this?' and agree a date to stop checking in.
try_team: In stand-up, each person names one task where they'd like less checking and one where they'd like more. Agree one change each; review in two weeks.

source.work: Manzoni & Barsoux, 'The Set-Up-to-Fail Syndrome', Harvard Business Review (1998)

hook: Your team hit the deadline. Will next month pay for it?
title: The Six-Week Bill

game.prompt: Six weeks later, does this fix hold or bite back?

items.text: The whole team works weekends to hit a launch date
items.why: Bites back as a habit: tired people make more errors, and fixing them eats next month. Once is fine.

items.text: Adding two new people to a project that's already late
items.why: Bites back: veterans stop to train them. Brooks saw this make late projects later.

items.text: Muting an alert that keeps going off
items.why: Bites back: quiet today, surprise later. The cause is still there, now unwatched.

items.text: A big discount to hit this quarter's sales target
items.why: Bites back: clients learn to wait for the discount, so next quarter starts weaker.

items.text: Spending a day finding why the same handover keeps failing
items.why: Holds: slower this week, but the problem stops coming back.

items.text: A one-page checklist for the step everyone forgets
items.why: Holds: cheap, and it fixes the cause (memory) rather than the symptom.

insight: Four of six bite back. Quick fixes ease the symptom now; the bill lands weeks later, so no one links the two. Repenning & Sterman saw whole teams stuck firefighting this way.
model: Before a quick fix, ask: what will this cost in six weeks, and who will pay?
try_today: Pick one fix your team keeps repeating. Spend 20 minutes asking 'why does this keep happening?' until you hit a cause you can change.
try_team: List three fixes from last month on a whiteboard. Everyone writes what each one cost later. Pick one to swap for a root-cause fix this sprint.

source.work: The Fifth Discipline (1990); Repenning & Sterman, 'Nobody Ever Gets Credit for Fixing Problems that Never Happened', California Management Review (2001); Brooks, The Mythical Man-Month (1975)

hook: New school, two months in, no real mate yet. Broken, or just early?
title: Friendship Runs on a Delay

game.question: Roughly how many hours of hanging out does it take to turn someone you know into an actual friend?
game.explain: About 90 hours, by one study's estimate: around 50 for a casual friend, 200+ for a close one (Hall, 2019, surveys of adults and university students). Time chatting and joking counted more than sitting in the same lesson.

insight: Two months of lessons might be only 10 hours of real talk. Friendship has a long delay, so 'nothing's happening' usually means 'not enough hours yet', not 'something's wrong with me'.
model: When results lag effort, count the hours you've put in, not the weeks on the calendar.
try_today: Pick one person you get on with and add 20 minutes of real hanging out: walk home together, share lunch, or play one game.
try_team: Class or club: pair up with someone you barely know and swap three fun questions for 5 minutes. Repeat weekly so the hours add up.

source.work: Hall, 'How many hours does it take to make a friend?', Journal of Social and Personal Relationships (2019)
